themes.theme: Institution-level and sector-wide monitoring of AI use and compliance
themes.definition: Mechanisms by which a public body, or the EU as a whole, monitors its overall use of AI, compliance with internal rules and the value delivered, rather than the performance of a single system.
themes.what_is_set_out: The European Parliament's administration 'will address inherent risks through continuous oversight during the entire lifecycle' of AI products and services (the same sentence appears in its 2020 and 2024 texts), its responsible services 'shall continuously address how rules and regulations are implemented', especially for AI Act risk levels, and dependency on external experts or service providers 'must be limited and monitored'. The Commission gives its internal AI governance the task to 'support and monitor compliance' with its operational guidelines, the ISG-AI the task to drive and monitor corporate implementation, and keeps a register of systems in use assessed against guidelines and legal requirements. The Court of Auditors will monitor its use of AI in audit work 'to ensure that human judgement remains central'. The JRC reports recommend national strategies with monitoring 'both at the national level and within individual administrations', monitoring by public administrations of public value through key performance indicators and of users' readiness, an EU observatory to monitor AI use in the public sector, LORDI-type indicators, and reuse of impact-assessment data by national and international authorities. These describe oversight of AI programmes rather than checks on individual outputs.
themes.holders: The Parliament's administration and responsible services; the Commission's internal AI governance, the ISG-AI and corporate governance boards; the ECA; Member States and individual administrations (JRC143539); public administrations and national and international authorities (JRC129100); a proposed EU observatory on AI.
themes.binding: Internal mandates and statements of intent ('will', and 'shall' or 'must' within internal frameworks) for EU institutions; recommendations and suggested options for JRC. No consequences are stated.
themes.checks: Trigger: continuous or ongoing; for national strategies, starting from an assessment of needs. Compared against: internal guidelines, AI Act risk levels and legal requirements; intended public value; European values and digital principles. Metric or threshold: key performance indicators (unspecified); LORDI-type indicators (coder note); otherwise not stated. Who: as listed under holders. Result: 'deciding if adjustments are needed' (JRC143539); otherwise not stated.

quotes.quote: Throughout the adoption process – and after deployment – public administrations should monitor whether AI solutions are delivering the intended public value, tracking progress through key performance indicators, and deciding if adjustments are needed.

quotes.location: page 3, II. Compliance and control, para 13
quotes.quote: Parliament's responsible services shall continuously address how rules and regulations are implemented, in particular concerning measures associated to the various levels of risks identified in the AI Act.
Establish and maintain an up-to-date register of AI systems in use at the Commission, assessed against corporate guidelines and legal requirements .
Any such use of AI will be carefully monitored to ensure that human judgement remains central to these key deliverables.

themes.theme: Checks carried out by regulators and supervisory authorities
themes.definition: Evaluations, tests and monitoring that market surveillance authorities, the AI Office, the Commission and data protection supervisory authorities carry out on AI systems, models or the operators responsible for them.
themes.what_is_set_out: Market surveillance authorities must evaluate a system against all the Regulation's requirements when they have 'sufficient reason' to consider it presents a risk (Art. 79(2)), or against Art. 6(3) and the Commission guidelines when they suspect a provider wrongly classified it as not high-risk (Art. 80(1)); they may run checks using EU database registrations (Art. 80(8)), verify real-world testing in sandboxes (Art. 76(2)), and must organise technical testing 'with the close involvement of the requesting public authority or body' where documentation is insufficient (Art. 77(3)). They also act as notified body for law enforcement, migration, asylum and EU-institution systems. The AI Office may evaluate GPAI models after consulting the Board (Art. 92) and is tasked with monitoring GPAI providers' compliance; the Commission and Board must 'regularly monitor and evaluate' codes of practice, the Commission will monitor the training-data summary template, and it must keep supervision data confidential; under the Omnibus the AI Office also conducts conformity assessments and tests for certain systems. The prohibited-practices guidelines require market surveillance authorities to investigate each case's facts when judging manipulation. For data protection, the EDPB tells supervisory authorities to evaluate case by case whether a controller's measures to make a model anonymous 'are appropriate and effective', looking at data-source selection, development measures, tests and documentation.
themes.holders: Market surveillance authorities; the AI Office; the European Commission and the European Artificial Intelligence Board; national data protection supervisory authorities (SAs).
themes.binding: Statutory duties and powers in the AI Act and Omnibus ('shall', 'may'); Commission guidelines and the EDPB opinion are interpretive ('must', 'should'). Consequences named in coder fields: corrective action, withdrawal or recall (Art. 79); for SAs, if anonymity cannot be confirmed the controller may be found to have failed its accountability obligations.
themes.checks: Trigger: sufficient reason to consider a risk or misclassification; a request from a public authority; sandbox testing; information on a GPAI model insufficient to assess compliance or a need to investigate systemic risk; regular review of codes; a claim that a model is anonymous. Compared against: all requirements of the Regulation; Art. 6(3) conditions and Commission guidelines; Art. 60 conditions; EU database registrations; the objectives of codes of practice; the appropriateness and effectiveness of anonymisation measures. Metric or threshold: not stated. Who: as listed under holders. Result: corrective action, withdrawal, recall or fines; otherwise not stated.

quotes.quote: it shall carry out an evaluation of the AI system concerned in respect of its compliance with all the requirements and obligations laid down in this Regulation
The market surveillance authority shall organise the testing with the close involvement of the requesting public authority or body within a reasonable time following the request.
SAs should evaluate, on a case -by-case basis, if the measures implemented by the controller to ensure and prove that an AI model is anonymous are appropriate and effective.
t he AI Office is tasked with monitoring whether providers of general-purpose AI models effectively comply with their obligations under the AI Act

themes.theme: Fundamental rights and data protection impact assessments before use
themes.definition: Assessments that a deployer or controller must carry out before putting a system into use, describing the use and assessing its impact on people's rights, and updating it when circumstances change.
themes.what_is_set_out: Article 27 requires deployers that are bodies governed by public law, private entities providing public services, and deployers of the systems in Annex III points 5(b) and (c) to perform a fundamental rights impact assessment before first use, describing the deployer's processes, period and frequency of use, affected persons and specific risks, and to update it when the deployer considers any element has changed. For law-enforcement real-time remote biometric identification, a completed FRIA and registration are preconditions for authorising use (Art. 5(2)); the Commission's guidelines bring the FRIA content forward for this use in the interim, asking it to identify affected rights and the severity and scale of impact, to 'describe the performance and accuracy level of the system', and to describe how outputs will be interpreted and verified by a human agent, and stress that the duty rests on the deployer itself. The FRIA 'should complement' and does not replace the data protection impact assessment; the Omnibus lets deployers cross-refer to the DPIA, and Art. 26(9) tells deployers to use the provider's information for their DPIA. EDPS's generative AI orientations require a DPIA before processing likely to result in high risk, regular review of risk assessments and a review at least when risks change, documentation of decisions across the lifecycle and mitigation of identified risks, and say developers and deployers may need their own risk assessments; the EDPB calls DPIAs 'an important element of accountability'.
themes.holders: Deployers that are bodies governed by public law or private entities providing public services, and deployers of Annex III point 5(b) and (c) systems (Art. 27); law enforcement authorities deploying real-time biometric identification; deployers as data controllers (DPIA); developers and deployers and all actors involved in a DPIA (EDPS); controllers (EDPB).
themes.binding: Statutory duty (Arts 27 and 5(2)); the coders note Art. 27 is not among the provisions fined under Art. 99(4). For biometric identification, use 'shall be authorised only if' the FRIA is completed. The DPIA is a statutory duty under GDPR and EUDPR as restated; EDPS and EDPB are interpretive. The coder field on what follows if DPIA risks remain unmitigated is truncated.
themes.checks: Trigger: before first use; on change as judged by the deployer; for real-time biometric identification, before deployment; DPIA before processing likely to result in high risk and review at least when risks change. Compared against: the fundamental rights of affected persons and the severity and scale of impact; the technical documentation and, where available, training and testing data for performance and accuracy; for the DPIA review, the processing as assessed. Metric or threshold: not stated (qualitative severity and scale). Who: the deployer itself; for biometric identification, the law enforcement authority. Result: precondition for authorisation of biometric identification; mitigation measures; documented decisions; otherwise not stated.

quotes.quote: deployers that are bodies governed by public law, or are private entities providing public services, and deployers of high-risk AI systems referred to in points 5 (b) and (c) of Annex III, shall perform an assessment

The FRIA should describe the performance and accuracy level of the system, based on the technical documentation and, if available, the training data on which the technology was tested and developed to prevent biases and discrimination.

quotes.location: Art. 1(13)(a), replacing AI Act Art. 27(4); p. 20
quotes.quote: the deployer may, when conducting the fundamental rights impact assessment referred to in paragraph 1 of this Article, include cross-references to the relevant sections of that data protection impact assessment
regular monitoring and reviews of the risk assessments need to be carried out, since the functioning of the model may exacerbate identified risks or create new ones.

themes.theme: Necessity, proportionality and safeguards for biometric identification and other sensitive uses
themes.definition: Case-specific checks before use, and safeguards after it, that the AI Act and the prohibited-practices guidelines set for law-enforcement real-time biometric identification and for permitted emotion recognition.
themes.what_is_set_out: For real-time remote biometric identification in public spaces, the guidelines describe 'a double necessity and proportionality assessment' before each deployment: first by the user within the FRIA, then by a judicial or independent administrative authority within the limits of national law. The balancing weighs 'the seriousness, probability and scale of the harm' that would follow if the system were not used against the consequences of its use for the rights and freedoms of those concerned. If an urgent use is not approved, 'all the data, including the results and outputs of that use, must be immediately discarded and deleted', together with any reference database built for that search; logs should show the authority that an urgent request was timely; and each identification must be verified by two competent persons before action (see the human-review theme). The guidelines suggest national law may regulate 'the minimum reliability, threshold used, and accuracy rates' of systems, but set no values. For emotion recognition in workplaces or education permitted on medical or safety grounds, necessity is to be assessed objectively against that purpose, not the employer's or school's needs, and a prior written expert opinion is suggested as a safeguard.
themes.holders: Law enforcement authorities deploying real-time biometric identification; judicial or independent administrative authorities; Member States (national law); unnamed assessors for emotion-recognition necessity.
themes.binding: Statutory conditions under Art. 5 restated with non-binding interpretation; consequences: authorisation refused so the use is not permitted, and mandatory deletion of data and outputs after a rejected urgent use. The emotion-recognition safeguards are 'should' and 'could include'.
themes.checks: Trigger: before each deployment or request; rejection of an urgent use (deletion). Compared against: harm if the system is not used versus consequences for rights and freedoms; the Art. 5(1)(h) objectives and national law; for emotion recognition, the medical or safety purpose and less intrusive alternatives. Metric or threshold: qualitative (seriousness, probability, scale); national law may set reliability, threshold and accuracy rates, with no values given. Who: the deploying authority, then a judicial or independent administrative authority; an outside expert for emotion recognition. Result: authorisation granted or refused; deletion of data and outputs if refused.

quotes.quote: a double necessity and proportionality assessment should occur prior to the deployment of any real -time RBI system in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement purposes

The use of the ‘real-time’ remote biometric identification system in publicly accessible spaces shall be authorised only if the law enforcement authority has completed a fundamental rights impact assessment as provided for in Article 27
all the data, including the results and outputs of that use, must be immediately discarded and deleted.
The necessity should be assessed on an objective basis in relation to the medical and safety purpose, and not refer to the employer’s or educational institution’s ‘needs’.

themes.theme: Human oversight built into system design
themes.definition: Requirements that systems be designed so that people can oversee them, understand their limits and resist over-reliance, and that oversight arrangements be identified before use.
themes.what_is_set_out: Article 14 requires high-risk systems to be designed, 'including with appropriate human-machine interface tools', so that they 'can be effectively overseen by natural persons' while in use, and splits the work: the provider identifies before market entry the measures it builds in and the measures 'appropriate to be implemented by the deployer'. Overseers must be enabled to understand the system's capacities and limits, detect anomalies and 'remain aware of' automation bias; Annex IV requires an assessment of the oversight measures, including technical measures to help deployers interpret outputs, and the recitals mention built-in operational constraints that the system cannot override. Real-world testing must be 'effectively overseen' by both provider and deployer. EDPS tells EUIs, 'as public authorities', to put safeguards in place against over-reliance leading to automation and confirmation bias, without saying what they are; JRC143539 and ENISA state the aim of maintaining human oversight, or keeping 'the human in the middle', as services and security tools are automated.
themes.holders: Providers (design and identification of measures); deployers (implementation); the natural persons assigned oversight; providers and deployers in real-world testing; EUIs (EDPS); public administrations (JRC143539, implied); not stated (ENISA).
themes.binding: Statutory (Art. 14; fines via Art. 16(a) and, for deployers, Art. 26), qualified 'as appropriate and proportionate'; recitals non-binding; EDPS 'should'; JRC143539 and ENISA state aims.
themes.checks: Trigger: before placing on the market (identifying measures); during use (oversight); throughout real-world testing. Compared against: the risks, level of autonomy and context of use (Art. 14, per coder note). Metric or threshold: not stated. Who: the provider designs; the deployer and assigned persons implement. Result: not stated in these passages.

quotes.quote: High-risk AI systems shall be designed and developed in such a way, including with appropriate human-machine interface tools, that they can be effectively overseen by natural persons during the period in which they are in use.
to remain aware of the possible tendency of automatically relying or over-relying on the output produced by a high-risk AI system (automation bias)
EUIs, as public authorities, should put in place safeguards to avoid overreliance on the results provided by the systems that can lead to automation and confirmation biases.

As services become more automated, it is crucial to maintain transparency, human oversight and accountability, in order to uphold public trust and meet auditability standards, in accordance with the requirements of the AI Act.

themes.theme: Human review of individual outputs before action, decision or publication
themes.definition: Requirements or commitments that a person checks a specific AI output (an identification, a prediction, generated text, a draft, a screening result or a security fix) before it is acted on or published, and the conditions on that review.
themes.what_is_set_out: The strongest rule concerns remote biometric identification: no action or decision on an identification 'unless that identification has been separately verified and confirmed by at least two natural persons with the necessary competence, training and authority' (Art. 14(5)), with the verifiers' identities logged and a carve-out for law enforcement and migration where law considers the rule disproportionate. The prohibited-practices guidelines require that a human assessment of crime risk be 'based on objective and verifiable facts' linked to criminal activity for the exclusion to apply, and that the biometric FRIA clarify the human agent's role in verifying and interpreting outputs. Under Article 50, human review decides when disclosure or labelling can be dropped: outputs 'properly reviewed and sent by humans', review meaning 'deliberate examination of the substance' by people with relevant knowledge and professional judgement, with fact-checking 'a minimum requirement', and the exception void after any later substantive AI change; the Code commits signatory deployers to human-review or editorial policies before publication. EU institutions set their own rules: Commission staff 'should always critically assess any response' from public generative AI for bias, factual errors and intellectual property infringement; the Court of Auditors limits AI in recruitment to 'a preliminary assessment' with human review and final decisions by selection panels, requires 'robust human oversight' of AI agents' outputs for reliable sources, completeness and freedom from bias, and keeps accountability for AI-assisted control results with staff; the Commission envisages staff reviewing and correcting AI drafts (a potential use case); the Parliament says its administration should remain able to examine how an algorithm produced its answers. EDPS lists human review of predictions as a possible measure and suggests auditing how analysts interpret outputs; ENISA recommends human-gated triage and flags verification of AI-generated code patches as a bottleneck.
themes.holders: Deployers of biometric identification (two verifiers); human assessors in law enforcement; deployers publishing AI-generated text and signatory deployers (Code); Commission staff; ECA staff, the Human Resources Directorate and selection panels; Parliament's administration; EUIs and data controllers (EDPS); defenders and system managers (ENISA).
themes.binding: Statutory for biometric identification (Art. 14(5), fines via Art. 99(4)); conditions for exceptions under Art. 50 in non-binding Commission guidelines, with fines if disclosure is wrongly omitted; Code commitments for signatories; EU institution rules are 'should always' or commitments with no stated consequence; EDPS and ENISA are possible measures or recommendations; the Commission use case is not phrased as a requirement.
themes.checks: Trigger: each identification (biometrics); each prediction (crime risk); before publication and again after any substantive AI change (Art. 50 text); every response (Commission staff rules); each preliminary screening (ECA recruitment); introduction of AI agents (ECA); incident triage (ENISA). Compared against: separate confirmation by a second person, otherwise not stated (biometrics); objective and verifiable facts linked to criminal activity; the substance and accuracy of content (fact-checking); reliable sources, completeness and freedom from bias (ECA agents); bias, factual accuracy and intellectual property (Commission staff); absence of new bugs (ENISA patches). Metric or threshold: none. Who: two competent persons; staff; selection panels; persons with relevant knowledge and professional judgement. Result: no action without verification; disclosure exemption applies or falls away; the final decision stays with the human body (ECA); otherwise not stated.

quotes.quote: unless that identification has been separately verified and confirmed by at least two natural persons with the necessary competence, training and authority
Fact-checking the accuracy of the content is a minimum requirement that should be part of that review .

quotes.location: page 2, section 3 (RISKS AND LIMITATIONS OF GENER…
quotes.quote: [Rule n°2] Staff should always critically assess any response produced by an online available generative AI model for potential biases and factually inaccurate information.
Any such use would be limited to a preliminary assessment, with human review and final decision‑making remaining fully with the selection panels

themes.theme: Explainability, interpretability and understanding of the system
themes.definition: Requirements that providers, users and institutions understand how a system works and why it produced an output, and the techniques suggested for achieving this.
themes.what_is_set_out: An AI Act recital says high-risk systems should be designed so that deployers can 'understand how the AI system works, evaluate its functionality, and comprehend its strengths and limitations'. The European Parliament goes further for its own use: 'The reasoning behind AI algorithms and decision-making processes shall thus be made transparent and understandable' so it is clear why a model made a recommendation, knowledge of a solution's inner workings must be available to providers and users before deployment, explainability is to be built into the user experience and model design with traceable data origins, and the administration 'should remain capable of analysing the evidence used by an AI algorithm'. EDPS treats interpretability and explainability as 'prerequisites' for EUIs' data-protection compliance and suggests documentation of architecture and data, techniques such as LIME or SHAP, and statistical analysis of outputs with an explanation of their rationale. The Court of Auditors calls the ability to 'understand, validate, and, where necessary, audit the algorithms' equally important as data quality. To whom an explanation is owed is not stated in any of these passages.
themes.holders: Providers (design, recital); Parliament's administration (named in one passage, otherwise implied); providers and users of solutions considered for deployment (EP2020); EUIs as controllers (EDPS); public institutions (ECA).
themes.binding: Recital (non-binding); EP 'shall', 'must' and 'should' in internal frameworks without consequences; EDPS non-binding interpretation and possible measures; ECA statement of importance.
themes.checks: Trigger: before deployment (EP2020) and ongoing ('remain capable'). Compared against: not stated. Metric or threshold: not stated; EDPS suggests statistical analysis of outputs and feature-attribution techniques. Who: as listed under holders. Result: not stated.

quotes.location: page 3, II. Compliance and control, para 14
quotes.quote: The reasoning behind AI algorithms and decision-making processes shall thus be made transparent and understandable so that it is then clear why a model led to a certain recommendation or suggestion.

quotes.location: page 6, Transparent and explainable Artificial In…
quotes.quote: Parliament’s administration should remain capable of analysing the evidence used by an AI algorithm and examine the means by which the algorithm produced its answers or actions.
Analyse the output of the AI statistically and explain the rationale of the results or lack thereof.
High-risk AI systems should be designed in a manner to enable deployers to understand how the AI system works, evaluate its functionality, and comprehend its strengths and limitations.

themes.definition: Conditions and duties for testing AI systems in real conditions or controlled environments before full deployment, and for validating pilots before scaling them.
themes.what_is_set_out: Providers may test Annex III high-risk systems (and, under the Omnibus, Annex I product systems) in real-world conditions before market entry, alone or with deployers, subject to conditions: informed consent that is dated and documented, with an exception for law enforcement where seeking consent would prevent testing; protection of vulnerable groups; effective oversight by both provider and deployer; and a procedure for prompt recall when testing ends. The Omnibus adds 'a mandatory real-world testing plan to be agreed' with the national competent authority. Inside sandboxes, significant risks identified during development and testing 'shall result in an adequate mitigation', failing which testing or participation is suspended, and reuse of personal data requires monitoring for high risks to data subjects, an isolated data environment, processing logs and a complete record of training, testing and validation with results; market surveillance authorities verify compliance. The Commission stresses that real-world testing is not exempt from Article 50, and gives the example of a municipality testing facial recognition with volunteers at a carnival, which 'must be fully compliant' unless done in a sandbox. JRC129100 encourages public bodies to experiment with AI for public services in sandboxes, including procurement through sandboxing, and JRC143539 calls for mechanisms to validate pilot outcomes before scaling.
themes.holders: Providers and prospective providers; deployers and prospective deployers (oversight during testing); national competent authorities and market surveillance authorities; public bodies and their agencies (JRC129100); a municipality (worked example); public administrations (JRC143539, implied).
themes.binding: Statutory conditions on a permission: testing may not be conducted if they are not met; the Omnibus testing plan is mandatory; sandbox risks unmitigated lead to suspension; Commission guidance interpretive; JRC encouragement and recommendation.
themes.checks: Trigger: before placing on the market; throughout testing; termination of testing (recall); end of a pilot before scaling. Compared against: the real-world testing plan and Art. 60 conditions; the requirements of Arts 8-15 (Omnibus Art. 60a); for sandbox data reuse, high risks to data subjects under data-protection law. Metric or threshold: not stated. Who: the provider; the deployer; the national competent authority agrees the plan; market surveillance authorities verify. Result: suspension of testing or sandbox participation where no effective mitigation is possible; recall at termination; otherwise not stated.

quotes.quote: Providers or prospective providers may conduct testing of high-risk AI systems referred to in Annex III in real world conditions at any time before the placing on the market or the putting into service of the AI system

quotes.location: Art. 1(25), inserting AI Act Art. 60a(5)(a); p. 25
quotes.quote: include the provision of a mandatory real-world testing plan to be agreed between the provider or prospective provider and the national competent authority or relevant authority
the planned testing must be fully compliant with the requirements for RBI systems in the AI Act , unless the system is tested in an AI regulatory sandbox
public bodies, and their agencies in all Member States are encouraged to experiment with new AI-enabled applications for public services in these sandboxes

themes.theme: Obligations on general-purpose AI model providers
themes.definition: Delivery duties on providers of general-purpose AI models, which may sit inside public-sector tools: documentation, copyright policy, model evaluation, systemic-risk management, incident tracking, cybersecurity and compute estimation.
themes.what_is_set_out: All GPAI providers must draw up and keep up to date technical documentation including 'its training and testing process and the results of its evaluation' (Art. 53, Annex XI), and apply a copyright policy, for each model and throughout its lifecycle according to the Commission guidelines; a downstream modifier's duties are limited to the modification. Providers of models with systemic risk must 'perform model evaluation in accordance with standardised protocols and tools reflecting the state of the art', including documented adversarial testing, assess and mitigate systemic risks 'continuously' and more thoroughly before key lifecycle decisions, keep track of and document serious incidents, and ensure an 'adequate' level of cybersecurity for the model and its infrastructure. Providers should estimate cumulative training compute before a large run and document their assumptions, method and uncertainty, with estimates expected to fall within a 30% error margin (coder note). Models placed on the market before 2 August 2025 have until 2 August 2027. Authorised representatives verify documentation; the AI Office monitors compliance and the Commission may evaluate models; providers outside an adequate code of practice may show compliance through a gap analysis. EU090 advises measures to keep illegal content out of training data, the Art. 50 guidelines encourage model-level transparency measures, and ENISA calls for risk mitigations for models with advanced cyber capabilities.
themes.holders: Providers of GPAI models; providers of GPAI models with systemic risk; downstream modifiers who become providers; authorised representatives; the AI Office and the Commission (monitoring and evaluation).
themes.binding: Statutory (Arts 53, 54, 55; fines under Art. 101 per coder notes, outside the passages); Commission guidelines interpret ('must', 'expected to', 'should'); EU090 advisory ('advisable'); Art. 50 guidelines encourage; ENISA recommends.
themes.checks: Trigger: in particular before first placing on the market (Recital 114); continuously and before key decisions (systemic risk); on serious incidents; before a large training run (compute). Compared against: standardised state-of-the-art protocols and tools; systemic risks at Union level; an adequate code of practice (gap analysis). Metric or threshold: not stated for evaluations; compute estimates within a 30% error margin. Who: the model provider; the AI Office or Commission for regulatory evaluations. Result: mitigation; documentation provided on request to the AI Office and national authorities; otherwise not stated.

quotes.quote: perform model evaluation in accordance with standardised protocols and tools reflecting the state of the art, including conducting and documenting adversarial testing of the model with a view to identifying and mitigating systemic risks
The systemic risk assessment and mitigation required under Article 55(1) AI Act must be carried out continuously for each model throughout its entire lifecycle.
Providers are nevertheless expected to document the assumptions made in making their estimations, including the method of estimation, and the associated uncertainties.
Such measures are advisable if the training data is likely to include illegal or unlawful content under Union law, in particular child sexual abuse material and terrorist content

themes.theme: Telling people they are dealing with an AI system
themes.definition: Article 50 duties, as interpreted by the Commission, to inform people that they are interacting with an AI system or exposed to emotion recognition or biometric categorisation, and how that information must be given.
themes.what_is_set_out: Providers of AI systems that interact directly with people 'must design and develop their systems' so that people are informed they are interacting with AI, 'effectively and consistently' throughout the lifecycle and at the latest at first interaction; AI agents must disclose 'both their artificial nature and the person on whose behalf they are acting', designed in 'at the architecture level' where contact with people is reasonably likely. Information must be clear and distinguishable rather than hidden in terms and conditions, manuals or menus; must be accessible to people with disabilities and take account of vulnerable groups; is recommended to be multimodal; must be given whenever the system is asked about its nature; and in 'riskier contexts', which the coders note include complaints handling, needs periodic reminders. Public bodies are directly concerned: AI police chatbots and hotlines open to the public 'remain subject to the transparency obligation', law-enforcement exemptions are assessed per deployment, and deployers of high-risk systems that make or assist decisions about people may combine their Art. 26(11) notice with Art. 50 notices. Deployers of emotion recognition or biometric categorisation must inform the people exposed. Human review removes the duty only for outputs 'properly reviewed and sent by humans as the main interlocutors'; a provider relying on the 'obvious' exception must assess and demonstrate obviousness to a reasonably well-informed, observant person.
themes.holders: Providers of interactive AI systems and AI agents; deployers of emotion recognition and biometric categorisation systems; deployers of high-risk systems that make or assist decisions about people; providers and deployers generally for the form and accessibility of information.
themes.binding: Statutory duties (Art. 50) restated in non-binding Commission guidelines, with fines up to EUR 15 000 000 or 3% of worldwide turnover (para 152); best practices only recommended.
themes.checks: Mostly not checks on tool outputs. Where an assessment is required (the 'obvious' exception; the law-enforcement exemption per deployment): trigger, before relying on the exception or at each deployment; compared against, a reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect person (the average-consumer standard); metric, not stated; who, the provider; result, the exception applies or disclosure is required. Human review of outputs as an exemption condition: see the human-review theme.

quotes.quote: providers of AI systems directly interacting with natural persons, who must design and develop their systems in such a way that the natural persons concerned are informed that they are interacting with an AI system.
AI agents must be designed and developed in such a way that they disclose both their artificial nature and the person on whose behalf they are acting
Such systems may be used , but they remain subject to the transparency obligation under Article 50(1) AI Act, so natural persons must be informed they are interacting with such systems.

require disclosure for the specific outputs in the interaction that are AI -generated, unless th ose AI outputs have been properly reviewed and sent by humans as the main interlocutors with the natural persons

themes.theme: Machine-readable marking and detection of AI-generated content
themes.definition: Duties on providers of generative AI to mark outputs in machine-readable form and make them detectable, and the testing of the marking and detection solutions themselves.
themes.what_is_set_out: Providers of generative systems 'must ensure that the outputs of the AI system are marked in a machine-readable format' and are 'detectable as artificially generated or manipulated content', with a combination of solutions that meets the legal requirements, which the recital describes as reliable, interoperable, effective and robust, and that is continuously adapted 'as the technology and state of the art evolves'. AI-generated summaries and substantive rewrites need marking; a narrow business-to-business exemption expressly excludes 'public and consumer-facing AI systems'. The Code of practice makes this operational for signatories: at least two layers of machine-readable marking (digitally signed, time-stamped metadata and an imperceptible watermark, except very short text), retention of existing markings, a detection solution available to deployers, competent authorities and others, detection results that state what they are based on, detection accuracy measured with metrics 'such as the error rate of the detection', adversarial robustness testing, testing 'prior to placing ... and regularly thereafter' under conditions representative of real use, and follow-up corrective action on reported shortcomings. One measure states that there is 'no quantitative evaluation metric' and relies on user-based assessment. Detection must respect data protection, including zero retention of uploaded content; forensic detection and fingerprinting are optional. Generative systems already on the market before 2 August 2026 have until 2 December 2026 (Omnibus), and providers outside an adequate code should carry out a gap analysis.
themes.holders: Providers of generative AI systems, including GPAI systems and agents; signatories of the Code who are providers; providers of open-source components and of GPAI and other generative models (encouraged); providers and deployers not adhering to a code (gap analysis).
themes.binding: Statutory (Art. 50(2)) restated in non-binding guidelines, with fines (para 152); Code measures bind signatories only ('will'), with compliance monitored by market surveillance authorities and no consequence stated; some measures optional ('may'); model-level and open-source measures only encouraged.
themes.checks: Trigger: before placing on the market or putting into service, then regularly; on changes in the state of the art; ongoing monitoring of reported shortcomings. Compared against: the Art. 50(2) requirements (effectiveness, reliability, robustness, interoperability); conditions representative of real-world use; a variety of content samples (coder note). Metric or threshold: error rate of detection, with no value set; for usability of detection, a user-based assessment with no quantitative metric. Who: the provider or signatory. Result: follow-up corrective action on substantiated shortcomings; documentation of the compliance process.

quotes.quote: First, providers must ensure that the outputs of the AI system are marked in a machine-readable format. Second, providers must ensure that the outputs are detectable as artificially generated or manipulated content.
Signatories will measure the accuracy of the detection of AI-generated or manipulated content by using relevant metrics for the type of markings, such as the error rate of the detection.
There is no quantitative evaluation metric linked to this Measure; instead, it requires a user-based assessment of the detection functionality.

it is appropriate to require providers of those systems to embed technical solutions that enable marking in a machine readable format and detection that the output has been generated or manipulated by an AI system and not a human

themes.theme: Labelling deep fakes and AI-generated text on matters of public interest
themes.definition: Deployer duties to label deep fakes and AI-generated or manipulated text published to inform the public, including the human-review exception on which public bodies may rely.
themes.what_is_set_out: Deployers must disclose that deep fake image, audio or video content is artificially generated or manipulated, with labels 'understandable and perceivable by natural persons' that do not depend on the provider's machine-readable marks; whether content resembles a real subject closely enough is 'a case-by-case assessment to be done by the deployer', and third parties' rights must be safeguarded even for artistic or satirical content. Deployers that publish AI-generated or manipulated text 'with the purpose of informing the public on matters of public interest' must disclose it, and public-interest topics expressly include 'public administration and services, the administration of justice and law enforcement', which the coders read as bringing much public-sector communication into scope [inference]. The exception for text under human review or editorial control requires deliberate examination of substance by knowledgeable people, fact-checking as a minimum, and a person holding editorial responsibility; any substantive AI change after sign-off voids it. Text generated before 2 August 2026 but published on or after that date must be labelled, while labelling of older deep fakes is only encouraged. The Code commits signatory deployers to processes that 'ensure and verify' labels are applied correctly, to documentation of how they disclose, and to human-review or editorial policies before publication.
themes.holders: Deployers of AI systems that generate deep fakes or text published on matters of public interest, which include public bodies [inference]; deployers relying on the human-review exception; signatory deployers (Code).
themes.binding: Statutory (Art. 50(4)) restated in non-binding Commission guidelines, with fines (para 152) and, for non-adhering deployers, possible requests for information; Code commitments for signatories, monitored by market surveillance authorities; labelling of pre-existing content encouraged only.
themes.checks: Trigger: each piece of content; prior to publication; again after any substantive AI change. Compared against: the substance and accuracy of the content (fact-checking); the simulated subject (deep fakes); the design and placement specifications for labels (Code). Metric or threshold: not stated. Who: the deployer; reviewers with relevant knowledge and professional judgement; a person with editorial responsibility. Result: label required, or exception applies; the exception becomes void after later AI changes.

quotes.quote: obliges deployers of AI systems that generate or manipulate text which is published with the purpose of informing the public on matters of public interest to disclose that such text has been artificially generated or manipulated

texts should be considered to address public interest matters if they cover topics on politics and democratic processes , public administration and services, the administration of justice and law enforcement
Any substantive AI intervention occurring after the human review or editorial control process has taken place will therefore cause the exception to become void.

All other Signatories, including those without such review or editorial procedures , commit to establish, adapt, or maintain appropriate policies for human review or editorial control prior to publication
